content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended the use of rapid diagnostic tests for tuberculosis (TB), particularly to enhance the capacity for investigating pediatric and extrapulmonary TB. This includes ensuring adequate staffing and maintaining updated contact details for healthcare providers. The Health Resources and Services Availability Monitoring System (HeRAMS) can play a critical role in updating TB service mapping in countries adopting this approach. Laboratory services are essential for TB prevention and care, as they provide the foundation for accurate diagnosis and guide treatment decisions. Due to technical requirements, quality assurance, and the need to optimize coverage, laboratory services are organized into networks at different levels of care. These networks utilize complementary diagnostic tools and are supported by a robust supply system. The implementation of new diagnostic tests, such as first-line and second-line line-probe assays (FL-LPA and SL-LPA), next-generation sequencing (NGS), and high-complexity reverse hybridization nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance, is increasingly important. These tests are suited for higher-level laboratories and can leverage existing infrastructure. Additionally, culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) using solid or liquid media should be available at this level, particularly for new and repurposed TB drugs. The structure of TB diagnostic networks and the testing packages available at each level should be tailored to meet the needs of the community and the local TB epidemiology. In many countries with moderate to high TB burdens, there remains a significant gap in access to WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostic testing for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB). Smear microscopy is still recommended for treatment monitoring in some settings, although novel specimen transport approaches are helping to address access challenges. Efforts to expand diagnostic resources have been a major focus of domestic and international funding for TB. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated the feasibility and importance of expanding access to diagnostic platforms capable of testing for multiple diseases, which is particularly beneficial for vulnerable populations. Mapping TB diagnostic services should also include facilities offering chest radiography, mobile diagnostic units, and other tools for TB diagnosis. Treatment services for TB are typically organized into three levels: clinic-based, community-based, and hospital-based care. Clinic-based care involves providing the full course of treatment on an outpatient basis at accessible health facilities. Community-based care allows patients to receive treatment in their own communities, supported by treatment supporters or community health workers. Hospital care is reserved for severely ill patients, including those with drug-resistant TB. Service mapping should account for the location, accessibility, capacity, staffing, and contact details of treatment centers, as this information is critical during emergency responses. Local health staff compiled lists of TB patients from memory when medical records were lost, and treatment centers were mapped and assessed for functionality. Facility maps were distributed to NGOs and foreign medical teams to facilitate the referral of TB patients to appropriate facilities. Within a month, nearly all TB patients in typhoon-affected areas were receiving treatment again. Preparedness for emergencies requires experienced professionals to confirm TB diagnoses and support treatment initiation or continuation. National TB Programs (NTPs) should identify emergency focal points and technical partners in advance for rapid deployment. Expertise in diagnostics, clinical management, infection control, procurement, supply management, and community care is essential. Emergency contingency planning should include dedicated support teams and enhanced district teams. Forecasting TB drug requirements should account for population needs, available stock, transport means, and regulatory requirements. The Stop TB Partnership’s Global Drug Facility (GDF) offers emergency grants to prevent stockouts during crises. A well-designed system for transporting biological samples to laboratories is also critical. Monitoring and evaluation of TB services must continue uninterrupted during humanitarian emergencies. Digital case-based reporting systems are increasingly being adopted, although some countries still rely on paper-based systems. Data collected during emergencies can inform real-time improvements in TB care and prevention. Community engagement is vital in emergency settings, as community leaders and organizations can help identify TB patients, support treatment adherence, raise awareness, and advocate for better access to TB services. Community health workers, particularly those from affected populations, play a critical role in linking health services with communities. WHO has developed operational guidance and tools for community-based TB care through initiatives like Engage-TB. In some settings, private and non-NTP public healthcare providers may already be involved in TB care. Public-private mix (PPM) models can be leveraged to serve populations affected by emergencies, provided they are well-functioning and include supervisory structures. These networks should not impose financial burdens on TB patients, given their vulnerabilities. Finally, NTPs and their partners should include a TB component in national emergency communication plans. Effective collaboration between emergency communication teams and NTPs is essential for ensuring timely and accurate dissemination of information during crises.
